doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: First Time Ever I Saw Your Face and Clint Eastwood's movie
summary: Atlantic would not release the song as a single until Clint Eastwood phoned to use it in Play Misty for Me. Dorn tells how the film and a New Orleans radio secretary's edit made it a hit.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: done with the second record and I get a phone call one morning. I go into the office, right, and this guy I work with Mark Schulman, he said, “Clint Eastwood’s on the phone for you.” So I thought it was like somebody goofing, right? So I get on the phone and I go, “hello, Clint?” and he goes, “yes.” I said, “listen I can’t really talk to you right now, I’ve got Winston Churchill on the other phone, can you call back later?”

Yeah. Well I thought it was somebody goof — why would Clint Eastwood call me? And then he goes, “hey listen” you know and I go woah, I go, “hello Mr. Eastwood.” It’s like that Simpsons guy that gets on the bus all the time. So he said, “listen I just directed my first film — oh and all the time, “First Time Ever I Saw Your Face,” all the jazz disc jockeys said anytime they put that record on the phones lit up at the station. So I went to the guys at Atlantic in the singles place and I said, “we’ve got to put this out, I mean the guys are telling me, I think we can cross it over to the R&B stations,” I had this great plan, you know, and everybody said like, “back to your office, kid.” They said it’s too long, it’s too slow, it’s too up, it’s too down, it’s too blue, it’s too green, it’s too everything, so they wouldn’t put it out. So now Clint Eastwood calls, right? He said, “I was driving to work this morning and I was listening to KBCA and I heard this song by Roberta Flack called ‘First Time Ever I Saw Your Face.’ And I bought the album and I saw you produced it and I’m calling you.” So I said, “why?” He said, “I just finished directing my first film, it’s called ‘Play Misty for Me.’” And he said, “I want to use that song in the montage scene that the whole movie builds to with he and Jessica Walter in the redwood forest. So I said, you know knock yourself out, Jack. Wow. We got a song in a movie. He said, “but I’m out of money.” He said, “I only have a thousand dollars.” And that’s not a lot of money to license a song. So I said, “no problem” I said, “you can have it for a thousand cents,” you know, like going to be in a movie, that song. So I go to Nesuhi and said Clint Eastwood called and I told him the whole story I just told you, “they only have a thousand bucks.” He said, “naah, a thousand bucks isn’t right.” He said, “we get much more for film stuff.” I said, “well it’s his first movie, he ran out of money.” Anyway so we had one of our few arguments and I actually won. I said, “well I’ll pay — what do you want to me to do” I said, “take my next three weeks salary, do whatever you want, we’re going to be in a movie.” Anyway it goes into the movie and next thing you know radio stations all over the country are getting calls for “First Time Ever I saw Your Face” from the Clint Eastwood movie, and it broke in New Orleans, break meaning it started taking off in terms of phone response and sales in New Orleans. So it was still too long for most radio programming. I mean one of the points I hope we get across today is how much luck, serendipity and just wandering aimlessly into a dream world can affect your reality, you know, or certainly mine. So we get a call from the pop

station in New Orleans that said we’re getting a hundred calls a day for this song, but it’s too long, we have like a three minute and ten second or some kind of time limit on AM radio. So all right I’ll edit it. So I edit it, and there was no overnight then, we sent it by special delivery to the radio station. I said, “what do you think of those edits,” you know, “fit your format?” So the guy’s hemming and hawing, I said, “what’s the matter?” He said, “well, my secretary listened to it and she doesn’t like the edits.” I said, “really? Your secretary doesn’t like the edits?” I got like Ralph Kramden, you know. I said, “well what would your secretary, how would she edit it?” So he said, “why don’t you talk to her?” So I got on the phone, I go hello secretary. She goes hello Joel. I said, “well what did I do wrong, lady?” And she said well here’s how you should edit it. So I said okay, so I went and edited it her way and she was a hundred percent right. I sent it back down and they said man, it’s unbelievable. So I didn’t even edit the record. A secretary in New Orleans edited — and Clint Eastwood was driving down the street, what if he had left three minutes later? You know, or something, and he missed the song — I don’t know. And that sold four million records and won a Grammy for Record of the Year, it skyrocketed her. And you know, if you want to know like how I do it? Like this.
